source1: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Roman Republic', Encyclopaedia Britannica online - https://www.britannica.com/topic/Roman-Republic
source2: Department of Greek and Roman Art, 'The Roman Republic', Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History, Metropolitan Museum of Art - https://www.metmuseum.org/toah/hd/romr/hd_romr.htm
notes: Republican institutions (magistrates, Senate, assemblies) continued unbroken from 509 to 27 BCE; 264 BCE is a periodization boundary (First Punic War). Q4: final plebeian secession and lex Hortensia, 287 BCE.

source1: R. E. Dolan and R. L. Worden (eds.), Japan: A Country Study, 'Kofun and Asuka Periods', Library of Congress Federal Research Division, 1994 - http://countrystudies.us/japan/6.htm
source2: Department of Asian Art, 'Kofun Period (ca. 300-710)', Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History, Metropolitan Museum of Art - https://www.metmuseum.org/toah/hd/kofu/hd_kofu.htm
notes: Kofun/Asuka is an archaeological/art-historical boundary (538 or 552, Buddhism); the Yamato kingship and court continued without break (Met extends Kofun to 710). Q4: Iwai rebellion in Kyushu 527-528.

source1: Department of Medieval Art and The Cloisters, 'Byzantium (ca. 330-1453)', Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History, Metropolitan Museum of Art - https://www.metmuseum.org/toah/hd/byza/hd_byza.htm
source2: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Byzantine Empire' (the eastern half of the Roman Empire) - https://www.britannica.com/place/Byzantine-Empire
notes: At Theodosius I's death (Jan 395) rule at Constantinople passed to Arcadius; eastern imperial apparatus continued unbroken. Database end 394 vs 395. Q4: civil wars against Magnus Maximus (388) and Eugenius (Frigidus, 394).

successor: United States (naval military government; UN Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands from 1947)
source1: Erwin N. Thompson (National Park Service), National Register of Historic Places Nomination: Truk Lagoon Underwater Fleet, NPS 1984 - https://npgallery.nps.gov/NRHP/GetAsset/NRHP/76002267_text
source2: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands' - https://www.britannica.com/place/Trust-Territory-of-the-Pacific-Islands
notes: At end the core (Tonoas/Dublon) was under Japanese mandate rule; Truk was bombed 1944, bypassed, and its garrison surrendered to US forces 2 Sept 1945; US administration, then UN trusteeship 1947. Database 1948 too late.

successor: Sumerian city-states continued (Early Dynastic III); Akkadian Empire from c. 2340 BCE
source1: Department of Ancient Near Eastern Art, 'The Akkadian Period (ca. 2350-2150 B.C.)', Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History, Metropolitan Museum of Art, 2004 - https://www.metmuseum.org/toah/hd/akka/hd_akka.htm
source2: Department of Ancient Near Eastern Art, 'Early Dynastic Sculpture, 2900-2350 B.C.', Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History, Metropolitan Museum of Art - https://www.metmuseum.org/toah/hd/edys/hd_edys.htm
notes: Archaeologically defined period of competing city-state dynasties with no region-wide central authority; 2500 BCE is an internal sub-phase boundary with continuity. Conventional period ends c. 2350 BCE with Sargon's conquest; database end date looks wrong.

notes: Britannica, following the Puranas: Kanva rule ended c. 28 BCE through the rise of the Deccan-based Andhra (Satavahana) Simuka. Puranic chronology and actual Satavahana control of Magadha are disputed; capital uncertain (Pataliputra or Vidisha).

successor: Russian Provisional Government, then Bolshevik Soviet Russia (RSFSR; USSR from 1922)
source2: Glenn E. Curtis (ed.), Russia: A Country Study, 'Revolutions and Civil War' and 'The Last Years of the Autocracy', Library of Congress Federal Research Division, 1996 - http://countrystudies.us/russia/8.htm
notes: February Revolution in Petrograd overthrew the imperial government; Nicholas II abdicated (March 1917), Provisional Government formed, Bolsheviks seized power Nov 1917. No external conquest of the core. Q4: Revolution of 1905.

source1: Dennis M. Hanratty (ed.), Ecuador: A Country Study, 'The Struggle for Independence', Library of Congress Federal Research Division, 1991 - http://countrystudies.us/ecuador/7.htm
notes: Spanish colonial authority at Quito ended when Sucre's Gran Colombian-led army (with Peruvian auxiliaries) won at Pichincha, 24 May 1822; Audiencia president surrendered, Quito joined Gran Colombia. Database 1830 marks Ecuador's later separation. Q4: Quito revolts 1809-1812.

source1: R. E. Dolan and R. L. Worden (eds.), Japan: A Country Study, 'Nara and Heian Periods', Library of Congress Federal Research Division, 1994 - http://countrystudies.us/japan/7.htm
notes: Emperor Kammu moved the same imperial government from Nara to Nagaoka (784) and Heian-kyo (794); no break in central authority. Capital actually left Nara in 784. Q4: Fujiwara no Nakamaro's armed revolt, 764.

source1: R. E. Dolan and R. L. Worden (eds.), Japan: A Country Study, 'Kamakura and Muromachi Periods' and 'The Rise of the Military Class', Library of Congress Federal Research Division, 1994 - http://countrystudies.us/japan/11.htm
source2: Department of Asian Art, 'Heian Period (794-1185)', Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History, Metropolitan Museum of Art - https://www.metmuseum.org/toah/hd/heia/hd_heia.htm
notes: Genpei War 1180-85: internal Minamoto warrior house defeated the Taira; Yoritomo built a new military government at Kamakura, court relegated largely to ceremony (fully subordinated after 1221). Some see dyarchy, hence T0 possible. Q4: Hogen/Heiji conflicts, Genpei War.
